tip: German has hunger rather than being hungry: 'Hunger haben', negated as 'keinen Hunger'.
'Dieser' takes the same endings as 'der', 'das', 'die', so neuter is 'dieses': 'dieses Formular'.
'Darf ich ...?' is the polite formula for asking permission to do something: 'Darf ich Ihnen meinen Mann vorstellen?'
Masculine and neuter nouns usually add '-s' in the genitive: 'Konzert' becomes 'dieses Konzerts' (of this concert).
'Ein' shows no gender, so the adjective carries it: 'ein kalter Wind', where 'kalter' takes the '-er' that 'der' would have shown.
'Werden' plus the past participle makes the passive: 'muss unterschrieben werden' = must be signed.
For a fixed location 'auf' takes the dative: 'auf dem Berg' = on the hill, no movement involved.
'Teils ..., teils ...' pairs two partial statements, partly one way, partly the other: 'Teils war es interessant, teils eher langweilig'.
Reported speech uses Konjunktiv I: 'sie sagte, sie wolle ... auswandern' = she said she wanted to emigrate.
To negate a noun with no article, use 'kein', not 'nicht'; masculine accusative takes 'keinen': 'keinen Alkohol'.
'Werden' plus an infinitive builds the future, and the infinitive 'schicken' drops to the very end: 'werde ... schicken'.
'Sich leisten' means afford and needs a dative reflexive: 'ich kann mir ... leisten'.
'Wegen' takes the genitive, so the article shifts to 'der': 'wegen der Prüfung'.
'Keinerlei' means none whatsoever and never changes its ending: 'keinerlei Erfahrung', 'keinerlei Ideen'.
'Während' takes the genitive, marking the noun with 'der': 'während der Arbeitswoche'.
City names plus '-er' form fixed adjectives that never take endings: 'Kölner Dom', 'Berliner Luft'.
'Teils ... teils' splits one thing into two parts, partly this and partly that: 'Teils war der Film spannend, teils eher vorhersehbar'.
Negate a possessive with 'nicht', never 'kein': 'nicht mein Koffer' = not my suitcase. 'Kein' is only for nouns with no article.
After 'mit', 'niemand' adds the dative ending '-em': 'mit niemandem'.
'Wurde' plus a past participle makes the passive: 'der Antrag abgelehnt wurde' means was rejected.
'Zuhören' splits apart and takes the dative: 'hörte ... den Sorgen ... zu'.
Superlatives usually add '-st', then an adjective ending before the noun: 'das aufregendste Erlebnis'.
Attach '-mal' to a number to say how often something happens: 'dreimal', 'viermal', 'zehnmal'.
'Teuer' drops its inner 'e' in the comparative: 'teuer' becomes 'teurer', not 'teuerer'.
'Sei' is Konjunktiv I of 'sein' and flags reported speech: 'er sei ... gewesen' means he claims he was.
'Weder ... noch' links two negatives, neither ... nor: 'weder Zeit noch Lust'.
German uses 'stehen' for things resting upright, where English just says is: 'Mein Fahrrad steht ... in der Garage'.
For a single completed past event, when is 'als', not 'wenn': 'als wir ankamen'.
This is accusative because it is short for 'ich wünsche dir ...': 'einen wunderschönen guten Morgen'.
'Auf Wiederhören' is the phone goodbye, from 'hören' (to hear); in person you say 'Auf Wiedersehen'.
